# The Moon Is Leaving

A few times a month, when the sky cooperates, observatories in New Mexico and France aim lasers at the Moon. They aren't pointing at the Moon generally — they're pointing at five small arrays of mirrors left on its surface by Apollo astronauts and Soviet rovers between 1969 and 1973. Retroreflectors bounce light straight back along the path it came, so a pulse fired from Earth finds its way home. The round trip takes about two and a half seconds. Measured over decades, that delay tells us the distance to the Moon to within millimeters.

And what it tells us is this: the Moon is leaving. It drifts away from us at about 3.8 centimeters per year — roughly the speed your fingernails grow.

It isn't fleeing, exactly. It's being pushed. The Moon's gravity raises tides in the oceans, and a fainter tide in the rock of the Earth itself — a subtle bulge aimed at the Moon. But the Earth rotates faster than the Moon orbits, so friction drags that bulge slightly *ahead* of the Moon's position. The bulge's extra mass tugs the Moon forward in its orbit, and the Moon responds the only way an orbit can: by climbing higher. Every nudge outward costs the Earth a little spin. Our days lengthen by nearly two milliseconds per century. The ledger balances perfectly — angular momentum is always conserved — but the accounting is written in tides, and it has been running for four and a half billion years.

Scale that up and the consequences stop being abstract. The dinosaurs lived under a larger Moon and shorter days. Whatever comes after us will live under a smaller one. And roughly 600 million years from now, something quiet and enormous will end: total solar eclipses. We currently inhabit a lucky accident of geometry — the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and also about 400 times farther away, so the two appear almost exactly the same size in our sky. When they align, the Moon covers the Sun precisely, unveiling the corona, the diamond ring, Baily's beads. No other planet in the solar system gets this show. But the Moon's slow departure means its disk keeps shrinking against the unchanging face of the Sun. One day — a day no one will witness — the alignment will come and the Moon will fall just short, and instead of darkness there will be a ring of fire. There will be a last total eclipse, and it will pass unremarked.

We treat the Moon as the very definition of constancy. Every love poem ever written leans on it. But constancy is a question of timescale. Across a human life, the Moon is faithful. Across the life of the solar system, it's already halfway out the door. Maybe that's the honest shape of things: even the most steadfast objects are leaving, just slowly enough that we mistake it for staying. The farewell will take longer than every language that has ever had a word for the Moon, combined. By the time it ends, there may be no one left to notice — which may be why the universe made it so slow. Some departures are only bearable at the speed of fingernails.

Actually, let me consider writing about the moon drifting away. It's factual: the Moon recedes about 3.8 centimeters per year, measured by bouncing lasers off reflectors left by Apollo astronauts. That's a beautiful concrete detail — retroreflectors placed by human hands still being used half a century later. And it opens onto themes: impermanence, the patience of measurement, the fact that even the most constant thing in human history — the Moon — is leaving, slowly. Structure:
1. Open with the laser ranging experiment — astronomers fire lasers at mirrors astronauts left on the Moon; measure distance to millimeters.
2. The finding: 3.8 cm per year. Roughly the rate fingernails grow. The Moon is leaving.
3. Tidal explanation briefly — the Moon's gravity raises bulges on Earth; Earth's rotation drags the bulge ahead of the Moon; the bulge tugs the Moon forward, boosting its orbit. **The Moon Is Leaving**

Twice a month, weather permitting, observatories in Texas and France aim lasers at a patch of sky where the Moon happens to be. They're aiming at five small arrays of mirrors left behind by Apollo astronauts and Soviet rovers between 1969 and 1973 — retroreflectors that bounce light straight back along the path it came. The round trip takes about two and a half seconds. From that delay, measured over decades, scientists know the distance to the Moon to within millimeters.

But the Earth rotates faster than the Moon orbits, so friction drags that bulge slightly ahead of the Moon's position. The bulge's extra mass tugs the Moon forward in its orbit, giving it a small boost, and the Moon responds the only way an orbit can: by climbing higher. Every push outward costs the Earth a little spin. Our days are getting longer by nearly two milliseconds per century. The ledger balances perfectly — angular momentum is conserved — but the accounting is written in tides.

And somewhere around 600 million years from now, something quiet and enormous will end: total solar eclipses. Right now we live in a lucky accident of geometry — the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and also about 400 times farther away, so they appear almost exactly the same size in our sky. When the Moon crosses the Sun, it covers it precisely, revealing the corona, the diamond ring, Baily's beads. No other planet in the solar system gets this show. But the Moon's departure means its disk keeps shrinking against the fixed face of the Sun. One day — a day no one will witness — the alignment will occur and the Moon will fall just short, and the corona will glow around a ring of fire instead of going dark. There will be a last total eclipse, and it will pass unremarked.

Reflection close:

We tend to think of the Moon as the definition of constancy... every love poem, etc. But constancy is a matter of timescale. On the scale of a human life, the Moon is faithful. On the scale of the solar system, it's already halfway out the door. Maybe that's the honest shape of things: even the most steadfast objects are leaving, just slowly enough that we call it staying. The farewell takes longer than every language that has ever named the Moon combined. By the time it's finished, there may be no one left to notice — which might be why the universe made it so slow. Some departures are only bearable at the speed of fingernails.

Hmm, that last line is decent. Let me refine wording throughout. Also double-check: "five small arrays" — Apollo 11, 14, 15 each had a retroreflector (three), plus Lunokhod 1 and 2 (two French-built ones) = five total. Yes, five. Observatories: McDonald Observatory in Texas (APOLLO is Apache Point in New Mexico actually; the main modern one is APOLLO at Apache Point Observatory, New Mexico; also Grasse, France — Côte d'Azur Observatory). Let me say "New Mexico and France" to be accurate — APOLLO is at Apache Point, New Mexico. Or just say "observatories in the American Southwest and France." Safer: "A handful of observatories."

Round trip time: average distance ~384,400 km, round trip ~768,800 km / c (300,000 km/s) ≈ 2.56 s. "About two and a half seconds" correct.

Millimeter precision: lunar laser ranging achieves ~millimeter accuracy nowadays. Correct.

Days lengthening: ~1.7-2.3 ms per century. "Nearly two milliseconds per century" fine.

Last total eclipse estimate: commonly cited figures range from ~600 million to ~1 billion+ years for the very last, with ~600 Myr often quoted for when totality becomes impossible (some say 620 Myr). I'll say "roughly 600 million years" — defensible.

Sun/Moon ratio: Sun diameter ~1.39M km, Moon ~3,474 km → ratio ~400. Mean distances: Sun ~149.6M km, Moon ~384,400 km → ratio ~389. "About 400 times" fine.

Baily's beads spelling: usually "Baily's beads" (after Francis Baily). I'll use that.

Also could mention that the recession rate wasn't constant historically — tidal basins change it — but that's extra detail; could add one clause: "the rate has varied over deep time as continents rearranged the oceans." Nice touch, optional. Keep it lean.

Length check: aim ~450-550 words. Format: title in bold or as heading, then prose paragraphs. Given it's free writing, a markdown title is fine since this renders in chat. I'll use a simple bolded or # title. Probably a modest heading.

One more consideration: should I add a brief intro line before the essay ("Here's a short essay...")? The user said "write freely about whatever you want" — diving straight in is cleaner and more confident. Just deliver the piece. Maybe no preamble at all. Yes, dive straight in.

Polish the draft now.

Final structure:
1. Laser ranging opening
2. The finding + fingernails line
3. Mechanism paragraph
4. Deep time: dinosaurs, future, eclipses ending
5. Closing reflection

Write final version with care for rhythm.
